newsitem.title: USA: USDA eases Karnal bunt rules in Southwest and Cal..
newsitem.headline: USDA eases Karnal bunt rules in Southwest and Cal..

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department said Thursday it amended its Karnal bunt fungus regulations to change the criteria for classifying regulated wheat areas, easing restrictions on growers in Arizona and California.

The USDA said it also eased the restrictions on the movement of grain and other regulated articles from additional areas in Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas that continue to be classified as regulated areas.

"This rule substantially reduces the size of the area regulated for Karnal bunt, which means that there will no longer be restrictions imposed upon the movement of regulated articles such as grain, seed, and straw from those areas released from regulation," the USDA said.

In a notice published in the Federal Register, the agency's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said the interim rule became effective on April 25. Public comments on the change would be accepted until June 2.

The action amends the agency's existing Karnal bunt regulations by adding the requirement that a bunted wheat kernel be found in a field before the field is designated as a regulated area. The agency also said it would modify the classification of restricted areas by establishing separate areas for seed.

"We are taking this action because tests currently available for use in identifying spores do not allow us to differentiate between small numbers of Karnal bunt spores and the spores of an as yet unnamed, but widely distributed, ryegrass smut," USDA said.

This action will have the effect of removing some areas in Arizona and California from the list of regulated areas and will relieve restrictions on the movement of grain and other regulated articles from additional areas in Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas.
Scientists told APHIS that a positive finding of Karnal bunt can now be made only when bunted wheat kernels are present, the agency said.

"The detection of spores alone does not now allow us to make a conclusive determination that Karnal bunt disease is present in an area," the USDA said. "That conclusion had an immediate effect on the States of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, and Tennessee, where grain in a number of storage facilities had been found to be contaminated with spores that appeared to be Karnal bunt spores, and on South Carolina, where seed from a seed lot contaminated with those spores had been planted."

Last month, USDA lifted all emergency action notifications affecting those states due to the fact that no bunted wheat kernels had been detected in those areas. In that same announcement, we stated our intention to develop a new regulatory standard for determining the presence of Karnal bunt that would apply to all parts of the United States.

USDA's announcement on Thursday amended the Karnal bunt regulations to make them consistent with the agency's determination that the detection of a bunted wheat kernel is necessary to confirm the presence of Karnal bunt.

USDA's list of regulated areas now includes the Arizona counties of La Paz, Maricopa, Pinal, and Yuma. A total of 21 farm fields in the counties was found with bunted wheat kernels during the 1996 pre-harvest surveys, and 103 fields were identified as having been planted with contaminated seed. Cochise, Graham, and Pima counties were removed from the list of regulated areas, and the size of the regulated areas in La Paz, Maricopa, Pinal, and Yuma counties was reduced, the USDA said.
The agency said it believed the disease was spread in Arizona through contaminated farm equipment because half of the spore-positive fields fell within nine square miles.
In California, the Bard-Winterhaven area of Imperial County and the Palo Verde Valley area of Imperial and Riverside counties were designated as restricted areas for seed, the USDA said.

The Bard-Winterhaven area was designated as a restricted area for seed because it abuts Yuma County, Arizona, and falls within a distinct definable wheat production area that includes fields in Yuma County that were planted with contaminated seed.
The Palo Verde Valley was designated as a restricted area for seed because 55 fields within the valley were considered to be positive for Karnal bunt.

In New Mexico, there are 106 fields located in Dona Ana, Hidalgo, Luna, and Sierra counties that were identified as having been planted with contaminated seed, the USDA said. Because there were no fields found to contain bunted wheat kernels in New Mexico--only fields planted with contaminated seed--there were no surveillance areas in the state.

In Texas, there were 24 fields located in El Paso and Hudspeth counties identified as having been planted with contaminated seed. No fields were found to contain bunted wheat kernels in Texas, the agency said.
Karnal bunt makes wheat smell bad and reduces yield and quality, but is not a health risk.
